example.answer: You save $20 and pay $60 at the register.
example.problem: A jacket costs $80 with 25% off. How much do you save, and what do you pay?
example.title: A 25% off sale

faqs.a: Multiply the price by the discount as a decimal and subtract. For $80 at 25% off: $80 × 0.25 = $20 off, so you pay $60.
faqs.q: How do I calculate a discount price?

faqs.a: Multiply the price by 1 minus the discount as a decimal. For 25% off, that is $80 × 0.75 = $60 — one step instead of two.
faqs.q: Is there a shortcut for sale prices?

faqs.a: Multiply the discounts, not add them. 20% then 10% off means you pay 80% × 90% = 72% of the price, which is 28% off — not 30%.
Only sometimes. A 25% discount on an overpriced item can still cost more than a fair everyday price elsewhere. Compare the final price, not the discount.
faqs.q: Is a bigger discount always a better deal?

howItWorks: A discount is just a percentage of the original price. The calculator turns the discount percent into a decimal, multiplies it by the price to get the amount you save, and subtracts that from the price to get what you pay. The one-step shortcut does it in a single multiplication: for 25% off, you pay 75% of the price, so multiply by 0.75 directly.

These are straightforward price estimates for shopping and budgeting, not financial advice. Always check whether tax is added before or after the discount where you shop, since that changes the final total.

Discounts stack by multiplication, not addition. If a store takes 20% off and then another 10% off the sale price, you pay 80% × 90% = 72% of the original price, which is 28% off in total — not 30%. This calculator handles one discount at a time; for stacked discounts, run the sale price through again with the second percent.
intro: Work out sale prices in seconds with this discount calculator. Enter the original price and the percent off to see how much you save and what you actually pay at the register.

mistakes.text: 25% off $80 is $20 off, not $25 off. The percent always applies to the price, so convert it to a decimal of the price first.
mistakes.title: Reading the percent as dollars

mistakes.text: Two discounts multiply: 20% then 10% off is 28% off total (0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72), not 30% off.
mistakes.title: Adding stacked discounts

mistakes.text: A $60 sale price after 25% off means the original was $80 ($60 ÷ 0.75). Dividing by the discount instead of what you pay gives the wrong answer.
mistakes.title: Working backwards from the sale price wrong

mistakes.text: Some stores add tax before the discount, most after. On an $80 item at 25% off with 8% tax, the order changes the total by over a dollar.
mistakes.title: Forgetting about sales tax
